subject: Behavioral Economics
title: The Baader-Meinhof Phenomenon
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Baader-Meinhof Phenomenon.

hook.text: You learn a new word and suddenly it appears everywhere. It was always there. You just notice now.

buildup.text: After buying a red car, red cars seem to fill every road. The count hasn't changed at all.

discovery.text: This is frequency illusion. Once primed, your brain flags matching info it used to ignore.

twist.text: Confirmation bias then kicks in. Each new sighting reinforces your belief that it's everywhere.

climax.text: The world didn't change. Your filter did. Priming rewires what your brain treats as relevant.

quiz.question: What causes the Baader-Meinhof phenomenon?
options: Your brain starts noticing what it was primed to see
Memory improves after learning something new

details.summary: The Baader-Meinhof phenomenon, or frequency illusion, is the experience of suddenly noticing something everywhere after first learning about it. A new word, car model, or concept seems to appear constantly once it enters your awareness, though its frequency has not changed.
details.whyItMatters: The frequency illusion creates false pattern perception that can distort decision-making. Investors who learn about a sector see opportunities everywhere. Patients who learn a diagnosis notice symptoms in everyone.
takeaways: New awareness creates the illusion of increased frequency
The actual frequency has not changed, only your attention to it has
Selective attention and confirmation bias combine to create the illusion

faq.question: Why is it called the Baader-Meinhof phenomenon?
faq.answer: A commenter in a Minnesota newspaper described learning about the Baader-Meinhof terrorist group and then seemingly encountering references to it everywhere. The name stuck as a label for the frequency illusion, despite having no real connection to the group.

faq.question: How does the frequency illusion affect decision-making?
faq.answer: It creates confirmation bias by making newly learned concepts seem extremely common. An investor who learns about cryptocurrency might perceive it as ubiquitous and inevitable, not because it is, but because their attention now selectively captures every mention.
